title: Start Here: What You'll Learn and Why
summary: See what this course covers and in what order, why each piece matters when you build for the web, and how to work through the lessons.
intro: Every website you've used, from a search page to a game in a browser tab, is built from the same few pieces. This course teaches you those pieces from the very beginning, so you can build sites of your own and fix them when they break. This first lesson is the map: what the course covers and in what order, why each piece matters when you build for the web, how the lessons work, and what you'll be able to do at the end. You don't need to know anything about code. If you can use a browser, and type a command when a lesson tells you what to type, you're ready.

steps.title: What a web page is made of
steps.body:
Before you learn to build something, it helps to see what it's made of. A web page looks like one finished thing, but it's put together from a few separate pieces, and this whole course is about those pieces: what each one does, how to write it, and how it reaches your screen.

## A page starts as text

Every web page starts as text: plain letters and symbols saved in files, like a note you'd type on your computer. Your **browser**, the program you open websites in (Chrome, Safari, Firefox, Edge, or another), reads that text and turns it into the page you see, with its headings, pictures, buttons, and colors.

The text is written in three languages, and each one has its own job:

- **HTML** says what's on the page: this is a heading, this is a paragraph, this is a link, this is a picture.
- **CSS** says how it looks: colors, sizes, spacing, and where each thing sits.
- **JavaScript** says what it does: what happens when you click, type, or scroll.

Picture a house. HTML is the walls and the rooms, CSS is the paint and the furniture, and JavaScript is the wiring that turns the lights on when you flip a switch. A house can have bare walls, and a page can skip CSS or JavaScript, but most pages use all three.

## The files travel to you

Those files don't start out on your computer. They're kept on another computer somewhere, one that stays on day and night. When you open a page, your browser asks that computer for the files, and copies of them travel to you over the internet. The computer that hands out the files is called a **server**, because it serves them to anyone who asks.

That trip happens every time you open a page, and it's where the course begins, because a page that doesn't arrive can't show anything, however well it's written.

## What a web developer does

A **web developer** writes those files and makes sure they work for everyone: that the page reads well on a phone and on a laptop, that someone who can't see the screen can still use it with a **screen reader** (a program that reads the page aloud), that it loads quickly, and that it keeps working when something goes wrong.

The part of a site that runs in your browser is called the **frontend**, and it's what this course teaches. The part that runs on the server, like the code that saves your order in a shop, is the **backend**. Hack University's backend courses teach that half, and they build on this one.

The three examples below show a few lines of each language, so you know what each one looks like. You don't need to understand them yet. By the end of the course, you'll read and write code like this easily.

examples.title: HTML: what's on the page
examples.prompt: A few lines of HTML: a heading, a paragraph, and a button. A page's HTML file holds text like this.
examples.code:
Hello!

This is my first web page.
examples.explanation:
Each piece of text sits between two **tags**, the words in angle brackets. `

` starts the page's main heading, and `

`, with a slash, ends it. `

` marks a paragraph, and `

examples.title: CSS: how it looks
examples.prompt: A CSS rule that styles every button on the page.
examples.explanation: A CSS **rule** picks things on the page and says how they should look. The `button` at the top picks every button. Each line inside the curly braces sets one thing: the background color, the text color, the space around the text (`padding`), and how round the corners are (`border-radius`). `px` stands for pixels, the tiny dots a screen is made of. With this rule, the button from the HTML example turns purple, with white text and rounded corners, and the HTML didn't change at all. That's the point of the split: HTML holds the content and CSS holds the looks, so you can change one without touching the other.

examples.title: JavaScript: what it does
examples.prompt: A few lines of JavaScript that make the button do something when someone clicks it.
examples.explanation: The first line finds the button on the page and gives it a name, `button`, so the lines after it can use it. The next line says: when someone clicks this button, run the code inside the curly braces. That code changes the button's words to Hi there!. Click it, and the words change at once, without loading a new page. That's how pages respond to people: they wait for something to happen, like a click, a key press, or a scroll, and then change what's on the screen. The JavaScript lessons teach how to find things on a page, change them, and react to what people do.

steps.title: The path through the course
steps.body:
Knowing where you're headed makes each lesson easier to place. When you learn how a browser draws a page, it helps to know you'll use that to make your CSS fast. When you learn HTML, it helps to know JavaScript will soon be changing it. So here's the whole path, in order.

```diagram course-path
Each stop builds on the ones before it, so take them in order.
```

It runs in three stretches. First you learn how pages reach you and how the browser shows them. Then you learn the three languages, one at a time. Last come the ways to get your work online quickly, and the tools teams use to go faster.

## 1. How the web works

What happens between typing an address and seeing a page: where a site's files live, what each piece of the address in your browser's address bar means, how your computer finds the right server among millions, and how the two talk. It comes first because everything else rides on it. When a page says it can't be reached, a picture doesn't show, or a form sends nothing, the cause is often here, and these lessons teach you to read the clues.

## 2. How a browser draws a page

What the browser does with the files once they arrive: how it reads the HTML, applies the CSS, and paints the result onto your screen, and how it does that again every time something changes. This explains why some pages feel slow or jumpy, and it's what lets you write pages that stay smooth.

## 3. HTML

How to write a page's content: text, headings, lists, links, pictures, and forms that people fill in and send. You'll learn to choose each tag for what it means, not how it looks, which is what lets search engines find your page and screen readers read it aloud.

## 4. CSS

How to make a page look the way you want: colors, fonts, spacing, and layout. You'll learn how the browser decides which of your rules wins when two disagree, how everything on a page is a box, how to put boxes side by side, and how to make one page fit a phone, a tablet, and a wide screen, in light and dark themes.

## 5. JavaScript in the browser

How to make a page respond. You'll learn the language itself from zero, then use it to find things on the page and change them, react to clicks and typing, get fresh information from a server without loading a new page, and remember things in the browser between visits.

## 6. Shipping your code

How your files get from your computer to everyone else's, quickly. You'll meet **npm**, which installs code other people have shared, and **Vite**, a tool that shows your site while you work on it and packs your files small when it's time to put them online. You'll also learn how browsers keep copies of files so a second visit is faster, and how to measure a page's speed.

## 7. Libraries and frameworks

Code other people wrote, so you don't start from nothing every time. You'll learn what tools like these give you and what they cost, then try three you'll meet at work. **Bootstrap** is a kit of ready-made buttons, menus, and layouts. **jQuery** is an older JavaScript helper that many existing sites still run. **Tailwind** is a popular way to style a page with short style names written right in the HTML. They come last on purpose: once you know what's underneath, you can see exactly what each one does for you.

## After this course

Hack University's other web courses build on this one. React, and then Next.js, are what many teams use to build larger web apps, and the backend courses (Express, FastAPI, Spring Boot, and Go APIs) teach the server's side. Each of them expects what you learn here.

steps.title: How the lessons work
steps.body:
Each lesson is built from the same few pieces, always in the same places. A few minutes on what they are will save you time in every lesson after this one. ## Lessons and parts Each lesson answers one big question, like what happens when you open a page, and it's split into **parts** that each answer a smaller one. Read the parts in order. Each leans only on what came before it, and every new word is explained the first time it appears, so a word you don't know is a sign to go back a part, not to give up. Every part starts with why its idea matters, then shows how it works, and the last part of a lesson ends with a **recap**, a short list of what to remember. The list of lessons shows each lesson's parts, and a part counts as read once you've opened it. The links at the bottom of a part take you to the next one. ## Code to read Lessons show code in boxes like this one, with colors that make it easier to read: ```html

Hello!

``` The button at the top right of a box copies its code, so you never have to retype it. Nothing runs inside a lesson: the code here is for reading, and you try it yourself in the Playground. Most parts end with **examples**. Each one has a sentence saying what it shows, the code, and often an **Output** box with what appeared on the screen when we ran it. Output is always real, copied from an actual run, never typed by hand. When you run the same thing, times, dates, and version numbers will differ, and that's expected. ## Diagrams When something is easier to see than to read, like a message traveling between two computers, a part draws it. Small numbered circles mark steps in order, and the text calls them step 1, step 2, and so on. A highlighted box is the thing the part is about. ## The Playground and its terminal The Playground is where you try things. Open it with the **Playground** button at the top of any lesson. It's a real folder on your own computer, shown in three areas: the **Explorer** on the left lists the folder's files, the **editor** next to it is where you write, and the **terminal** underneath is where you run commands. A **terminal** is a window where you tell your computer what to do by typing instead of clicking. You type a command, press Enter, and the computer prints its answer underneath. A lesson shows each command in a box of its own, like the one below, with what it printed in the box after it. Try this one. It asks **Node.js**, a program that runs JavaScript, which you installed along with Hack University, which version it is: ```bash node --version ``` ```text v24.11.1 ``` Your number may be different, and that's fine. What you run in the Playground runs on your computer for real, the same as in any terminal window. Some lessons need two terminals at once: a server running in one, and commands that talk to it in the other. For the second one, use your computer's own terminal, the one you used to start Hack University: **Terminal** on a Mac (press Command and Space, then type Terminal), or **Command Prompt** on Windows. ## Your browser's developer tools Every browser comes with **developer tools**, called **DevTools** for short, that show what a page is made of and what it's doing behind the scenes. Open them with F12, or with Command, Option, and I on a Mac. In Safari, first turn on Show features for web developers, in Settings under Advanced. The lessons use DevTools often. ## What you'll be able to do By the end of the course, you'll be able to: - Explain what happens between typing an address and seeing a page, and find which step broke when one doesn't load. - Write HTML pages and forms that work for everyone, including people using screen readers. - Style pages with CSS that fit any screen, in light and dark themes. - Make pages respond with JavaScript, and get fresh information from servers. - Run a site with Vite while you build it, then pack it up to go online. - Pick up Bootstrap, jQuery, or Tailwind on a team that uses them. The next lesson starts at the very beginning: what a website is made of.

recap:
- A web page is text in three languages: HTML for what's on it, CSS for how it looks, and JavaScript for what it does.
- A page's files live on a server, a computer that stays on, and travel to your browser each time you open the page.
- The course goes in order: how the web works, how a browser draws a page, HTML, CSS, JavaScript, shipping your code, then libraries.
- Each part says why before how, and explains every new word the first time it appears.
- Code in a lesson is for reading and copying, and its output is always real.
- The Playground is a folder on your computer with an editor and a terminal, where you try what you read.
